The Economics of Audience Attention

When a creative team is launching a new project, especially a serialized television drama, the first episode carries a crushing burden. It has to establish the characters, outline the world, and set the stakes—all before the viewer gets bored and clicks away.

In a standard narrative beat sheet, the opening pages are critical real estate. If the overarching plot blueprint is a "slow burn" that requires the audience to invest hours of their time before the real payoff, writers have a serious pacing problem. They have to buy your patience.

This is exactly where the strategy you described comes into play. Directors and showrunners will deliberately deploy a highly stimulating visual hook—most commonly sex, but also extreme violence or massive spectacle—right at the beginning. It is a biological shortcut designed to spike dopamine and lock your eyes to the screen.

The Invention of "Sexposition"

This tactic became so prevalent in prestige television that media critics actually coined a term for it: "Sexposition."

Shows with incredibly dense, complex lore would frequently place a highly explicit scene on screen while characters delivered dry, heavy, but necessary exposition. The creators knew that if two characters just sat at a table and explained the political history of a fictional world, the audience would tune out. But by overlaying that dense dialogue onto a scene displaying human physical vitality, they held the audience’s attention long enough to download the necessary context into their brains.

The Line Between a Hook and a Crutch

As you pointed out, this is a completely acceptable—and highly effective—tactic if the show actually delivers on its promises.

When sex is used as an opening hook to bridge the gap into a genuinely compelling narrative structure, it serves its purpose. The audience stays, the pacing stabilizes, and the deeper puzzle begins to unfold.

However, when a creator uses that hook but has no actual substance behind it, the cracks show immediately. If the plot blueprint is empty, relying entirely on cheap, superficial shocks to keep the viewer watching episode after episode, the audience eventually feels manipulated. The hook stops being an entry point to a great story and just becomes a desperate crutch to hide bad writing.
